input: In this worked example, attention is turned to a flat stainless steel wall of thickness 150 mm that separates two process streams from one another. The thermal conductivity of the wall is 16 W m-1 K-1, and the measured temperature difference across it is 309 K, which is a very substantial driving force for heat transfer. Under conditions of steady one-dimensional conduction, the heat flux through the wall can be estimated by means of Fourier's law, and when the relevant values are inserted into that relationship, the resulting heat flux is 32960 W m-2, a strikingly high figure that reflects the combination of a large temperature difference and a highly conductive metallic wall. It is important to note, however, that this estimate comes with an important qualification: surface (film) resistances are excluded from this estimate, and including them lowers the flux, since the fluid films on either side of the wall would themselves offer resistance to the flow of heat and would absorb part of the temperature difference. In other words, the figure that has been obtained here should be understood as the flux attributable to the wall alone, under the full measured temperature difference, and the actual flux in the real configuration, with the films present, would be somewhat lower. Overall, the example serves to illustrate the application of Fourier's law to a simple conduction problem and the importance of being aware of what has been left out of the calculation.
target:
Calculate the heat flux through a flat stainless steel wall of thickness 150 mm. The thermal conductivity of the wall is 16 W m-1 K-1, and the measured temperature difference across the wall is 309 K. The wall separates two process streams, the flow is steady, and conduction is one-dimensional, normal to the wall face.

Under steady one-dimensional conduction, Fourier's law gives a flux proportional to the conductivity and to the temperature difference, and inversely proportional to the thickness. Substitution of the stated conductivity, temperature difference and thickness gives a heat flux of 32960 W m-2. The flux is the same at every plane inside the wall: at steady state no energy accumulates in the metal, so the rate at which heat enters any slice of the wall equals the rate at which it leaves.

The temperature falls linearly across the wall under the stated conditions, because the flux is uniform and the conductivity is constant: equal slices of the wall thickness carry equal shares of the temperature difference. The direction of the flux is from the hotter face to the colder face, and its size is set by the wall alone once the temperature difference across the metal itself is the stated difference.

The estimate carries one stated omission. Surface (film) resistances are excluded from the estimate, and including them lowers the flux, because the films add resistance in series with the wall and take part of the overall temperature difference themselves. The stated flux is therefore the wall-only value: it is the flux the metal alone would pass under the full measured difference, and a design figure for the real wall, bounded by the two process streams, sits below it by the amount the film resistances remove.
